headings.title: Introduction and Overview of Uterine Cancer
headings.content: Uterine cancer primarily develops in the inner lining of the uterus, known as the endometrium. It stands as one of the most frequently diagnosed gynecological malignancies, particularly affecting women after menopause. While endometrial carcinoma accounts for the vast majority of cases, rarer forms such as uterine sarcomas can also arise from the myometrium or supporting connective tissues. Early detection generally yields a favorable prognosis because symptoms like abnormal bleeding usually manifest in the initial stages, prompting women to seek medical evaluation. Understanding the broader epidemiological context helps healthcare providers recognize vulnerable populations, especially in resource-limited settings where delayed presentation remains a significant clinical challenge.

headings.title: Types and Classifications
headings.content:
Uterine malignancies are broadly categorized based on their cellular origin and behavior. 

- **Endometrial Adenocarcinoma**: Accounts for over 80 percent of cases, typically driven by estrogen exposure. Subtypes include endometrioid, serous, and clear cell carcinomas.
- **Uterine Sarcomas**: Rare mesenchymal tumors arising from the myometrium or endometrial stroma, including leiomyosarcomas and endometrial stromal sarcomas, which generally carry a more aggressive clinical course.

Type I tumors are usually low-grade and estrogen-dependent, whereas Type II tumors are high-grade, estrogen-independent, and associated with a poorer prognosis regardless of stage.

headings.title: Risk Factors and Etiology
headings.content:
The development of uterine cancer is strongly linked to prolonged, unopposed estrogen exposure. When estrogen stimulates the endometrium without adequate balancing progesterone, cellular proliferation increases, raising the risk of malignant mutations.

- **Obesity**: Adipose tissue converts androgen precursors to estrogen, serving as a major endogenous source.
- **Nulliparity and Infertility**: Continuous ovulatory cycles without the progesterone break provided by pregnancy increase cumulative exposure.
- **Late Menopause**: Menopause occurring after age 55 prolongs total lifetime estrogen exposure.
- **Tamoxifen Use**: Used in breast cancer treatment, it acts as an estrogen agonist on the endometrium.
- **Genetics**: Inherited syndromes like Lynch syndrome significantly elevate lifetime risk.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Assessment
headings.content: The hallmark symptom of uterine cancer is abnormal uterine bleeding. In postmenopausal women, any vaginal spotting or bleeding—no matter how minor—is considered suspicious and warrants immediate investigation. Pre-menopausal women may experience intermenstrual bleeding, menorrhagia, or increasingly irregular cycles. As the disease advances, patients might report pelvic pain, pressure, dyspareunia, or a palpable pelvic mass. A thorough nursing history must assess bleeding patterns, duration, and associated systemic signs like unexplained weight loss and fatigue, which suggest advanced disease or metastasis.

headings.title: Diagnostic Investigations
headings.content: Diagnosing uterine cancer involves a stepwise clinical evaluation. Transvaginal ultrasonography is often the initial imaging modality to measure endometrial thickness; a thickened stripe warrants further tissue sampling. Endometrial biopsy can be performed safely in an outpatient setting to obtain histological confirmation. When office biopsy results are inconclusive or symptoms persist despite a negative sample, fractional dilation and curettage combined with hysteroscopy is performed under anesthesia to visualize the uterine cavity directly. Once malignancy is confirmed, computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging assists in evaluating local invasion and distant metastasis.

headings.title: Medical and Surgical Management
headings.content: Surgical intervention serves as the cornerstone of treatment for localized uterine cancer. A total hysterectomy combined with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is standard practice, often accompanied by pelvic and para-aortic lymph node staging. Depending on surgical pathology findings and tumor grade, adjuvant therapy may be introduced. Radiation therapy, delivered via external beam or brachytherapy, reduces local recurrence rates. Systemic treatments such as chemotherapy or targeted hormonal therapies are utilized for advanced, recurrent, or high-risk aggressive histologic subtypes.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Patient Education
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing care addresses both the physical recovery and emotional well-being of a patient undergoing treatment for uterine cancer. Postoperative monitoring focuses on assessing vaginal bleeding, managing acute pain, and preventing complications like deep vein thrombosis through early ambulation and pneumatic compression devices. Education regarding surgical menopause—if ovaries are removed—helps patients anticipate vasomotor symptoms and bone density concerns. Nurses also provide guidance on pelvic rest guidelines, wound care, and recognizing signs of infection or lymphedema.

headings.title: Complications and Prognosis
headings.content: The prognosis of uterine cancer depends heavily on the stage at diagnosis, tumor grade, and histological subtype. Localized disease carries a very high long-term survival rate, whereas metastatic disease involving distant organs presents significant treatment challenges. Potential complications arising from the disease or its treatment include chronic lymphedema of the lower extremities due to lymph node dissection, bowel obstruction from radiation adhesions, sexual dysfunction, and psychological distress. Regular follow-up appointments are essential to monitor for recurrence and support survivorship health.
